title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Two-Wheelers Starting 2028. Here's the Full Electrification Timeline.
excerpt: The capital's new EV policy commits ₹15,000 crore, phases out fossil-fuel registration for autorickshaws by January and two-wheelers by April 2028, and aims for 95% electric new-vehicle registrations by 2027
body:
Delhi has tried everything to fix its air. Water trucks spraying mist. Odd-even licence plate schemes. Crop-burning bans that nobody enforces. None of it has made a noticeable dent in the city's pollution, which routinely exceeds the World Health Organization's safe limits by a factor of 20.

Now the capital is trying something that can't be ignored: banning new fossil-fuel two-wheelers and autorickshaws entirely.

The Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy 2026, notified on July 1 by Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu after cabinet approval by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, lays out the most aggressive electrification roadmap any Indian state has attempted. It took effect immediately and will remain in force until March 31, 2030.


## The Timeline: What Gets Banned and When

The policy is built around two hard deadlines that will reshape how Delhi moves.

**January 1, 2027**: Only electric autorickshaws and N1-category goods vehicles (small commercial trucks up to 3.5 tonnes) will be eligible for new registration in Delhi. No new petrol, diesel, or CNG three-wheelers will be registered after this date.

**April 1, 2028**: Only electric two-wheelers will be eligible for new registration. The sale and registration of new petrol and CNG scooters and motorcycles in Delhi will effectively end.

Existing vehicles are not affected. If you already own a petrol scooter or an old autorickshaw, you can keep driving it. The bans apply only to new registrations — a distinction that matters for Delhi's millions of existing two-wheeler owners.



> **"The bans apply only to new registrations — a distinction that matters for Delhi's millions of existing two-wheeler owners."**


## The Money: ₹15,000 Crore Over Four Years

The government is backing the mandate with serious money. The policy commits ₹15,000 crore (approximately $1.6 billion) across four years for incentives, charging infrastructure, and ecosystem support.

**Purchase incentives** are structured on a declining scale to reward early adopters:
- Electric two-wheelers: ₹30,000 in the first year, ₹20,000 in the second, ₹10,000 in the third
- Electric autorickshaws: ₹50,000 in the first year, ₹40,000 in the second, ₹30,000 in the third
- Electric goods vehicles (N1 category): Up to ₹1 lakh in the first year


![World Health Organization — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/World_Health_Organization_%40_Pregny-Chamb%C3%A9sy_%2850636746028%29.jpg/3840px-World_Health_Organization_%40_Pregny-Chamb%C3%A9sy_%2850636746028%29.jpg)


All incentives will be disbursed through Direct Benefit Transfer, cutting out intermediaries.

**Scrappage incentives** add another layer: owners who scrap old vehicles and switch to EVs can receive up to ₹1 lakh for four-wheelers, ₹50,000 for commercial trucks, ₹25,000 for three-wheelers, and ₹10,000 for two-wheelers. More than ₹1,500 crore has been earmarked specifically for scrappage.

**Tax breaks** round out the package: electric cars priced up to ₹30 lakh get a 100% exemption on road tax and registration fees.

## No Hybrids Allowed

One notable exclusion: hybrid vehicles are not eligible for any incentive under the policy. An earlier draft released in April had included hybrid support, but the final version dropped it entirely, focusing exclusively on battery electric vehicles.

The decision will disappoint automakers like Toyota and Maruti Suzuki that have pushed hybrids as a pragmatic bridge technology. But Delhi's logic is straightforward: if the goal is zero tailpipe emissions, half-measures dilute the mandate.

## 30,000 Charging Points

The infrastructure plan calls for more than 30,000 public charging points across the city, along with fast-charging corridors and battery-swapping stations. Residential and commercial buildings will be encouraged to install charging facilities, creating an ecosystem that makes EV ownership practical — not just aspirational.

## Why It Matters Beyond Delhi

Delhi is India's third-largest automotive market. Any policy that reshapes buying behaviour here sends ripple effects through the entire industry. Automakers have already responded positively, with several noting that the long-term roadmap provides the planning certainty they need to invest in electric product lines for the Indian market.

If executed well, the policy could become a template for other state governments wrestling with the same air quality crisis. The target is staggering: 95% of all new vehicle registrations in Delhi to be electric by 2027.

For the diaspora, the policy addresses something deeply personal. Anyone who has landed at IGI Airport and stepped into Delhi's winter smog knows the visceral shock. A study in *The Lancet Planetary Health* estimated 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution. Vehicular emissions contribute more than half of Delhi's pollution, according to the Centre for Science and Environment.

Delhi's EV mandate won't fix the air overnight. But for the first time, it puts a hard date on when the city's most polluting vehicle categories will stop growing — and that's more than any mist-spraying truck has ever promised.
